extracted.intended_audience: Spanish colonial officials, Council of the Indies, and colonial administrators
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance and procedural standards concerning conquest, tribute, treatment of natives, and colonial administration in the Spanish Philippines (mid-16th century), aimed at governors, clergy, and royal officials. Includes specific recommended tribute amounts, rules on legitimacy of conquest, reporting obligations to the King, and administrative financial rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royal mandate required for conquest
rubrics_metrics.description: No governor or captain may lawfully make conquest without an express mandate from His Majesty; except in cases of war waged in defense of persons or property, other conquests are unjust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fray Martin de Rada argues that 'no governor or captain can do so without an express mandate for it from his Majesty,' and that conquests made by force without such mandate are unjust even if causes exist. Reference is made to a letter specifying that the King ordered against making conquests in these islands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tribute must be minimal and proportionate
rubrics_metrics.description: Tribute as then imposed (three maez per Indian) is excessive and oppressive; the minimum fair tribute should be limited to one maez in food and raiment, or in other statements a small amount of rice (seventy gantas) and a piece of cloth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fray Martin recommends reducing tribute to the least amount possible for support—specifically one maez of food and clothing—or the earlier suggested 70 gantas of rice and one piece of cloth; he justifies reduction by the natives' poverty and subsistence on roots. This is offered as a temporary measure until the land and tools improve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tribute must not be extorted by force or imprisonment
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unjust to demand tribute by force (arquebuses, imprisonment), to keep chiefs or timaguas imprisoned to extract tribute, or to burn houses to coerce payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fray Martin condemns practices where tribute is exacted with weapons or by imprisoning chiefs; he provides anti-pattern examples: demolishing houses to avoid payment, demanding tribute with arquebuses, imprisoning chiefs in stocks. Those methods are characterized as cruelty and oppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reports to the King should be true, simple, and clear
rubrics_metrics.description: Officials should send to His Majesty a truthful, simple, and clear report of the methods used in the conquest, the present condition of the land, and methods adopted in collecting tributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fray Martin urges 'a true, simple, and clear report, without dissimulations' so the King can decree what ought to be done. This is presented as both a moral and practical requirement for royal oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repartimientos/encomiendas only justified to prevent greater injury
rubrics_metrics.description: Allotting land into repartimientos/encomiendas may be permissible to avoid robbery and disorder, but should not be assumed just by default and must be accompanied by safeguards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fray Martin acknowledges that, given current circumstances, allotment may be kept to support residents, but insists it must avoid greater injury, and that the natives must be protected and treated justly; he criticizes allotments founded on false information about voluntary submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Those who advise, execute, or fail to prevent abuses share responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Responsibility for unjust tribute, robberies, and other injuries rests not only on those who execute them but also on those who advise, send, or fail to prevent or make restitution for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fray Martin enumerates culpable parties: the person who orders tribute, the captain, soldiers participating, advisers, and those who could prevent or make restitution but do not. This is presented as a standard of moral/legal accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect natives and secure justice and instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Where Spaniards maintain control, they should protect natives from enemies, maintain justice, and provide religious instruction rather than subjecting them to exploitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fray Martin stresses that reform must include protection from pirates and injustice, and that religious instruction and justice are part of the proper relationship; lack of such protection undermines any claim of rightful subjugation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxation specifics in Manila (local levy standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the island (Manila) taxation imposed: each tributario must annually pay a piece of cotton cloth (about ten varas long and two varas wide), two arrobas of rice, and one hen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is described as a practical imposition that can be levied without difficulty due to abundance of such items; presented as the current local standard for tribute in that settlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office appointment income must serve common welfare
rubrics_metrics.description: Income and fees attached to the office of corredor de Lonxa shall be enjoyed by the appointed persons but the income which they give each year must be for the estates of the city and expended for the common welfare, not for other purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Royal decree grants the office and its jurisdiction analogous to other corredores de Lonxa, but explicitly directs that income be used for common welfare; appointment method left to the city but constrained by this fiscal rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial diplomatic approach: offer peace, assurances, and presents
rubrics_metrics.description: Before resorting to force, governors should approach natives with assurances of safety, gifts, and offers of friendship to facilitate peaceful submission and trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The governor's practice is given as example: sending a spy to ascertain intentions, explaining peaceful aims, giving presents, and receiving chiefs in person; such measures often reassured natives and led to peace without bloodshed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider natives' capacity and avoid measures causing destitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Tribute and demands must consider natives' real capacity: many subsist barely and are unable to pay large impositions without demolishing houses or fleeing; excessive tribute causes destitution and flight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fray Martin documents that many natives live part of the year on roots and cannot support heavy tribute; he uses this to argue for minimal tribute and for Spaniards to aid where possible rather than extract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-defense and proportional military response
rubrics_metrics.description: When Spaniards are attacked (e.g., by artillery), self-defense and proportionate military action are justified; individual excesses in conduct should be judged separately from royal policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Reply argues that in instances where natives fired upon Spaniards, entering and subduing cities was done in self-defense and security (e.g., burning city to protect small number of Spaniards). It also frames excesses as individual faults rather than evidence of improper royal instructions.
